questions.question_text:
The corners and mid-points of the sides of a triangle are named using the distinct
letters P, Q, R, S, T and U, but not necessarily in the same order. Consider the
following statements:
 The line joining P and R is parallel to the line joining Q and S.
 P is placed on the side opposite to the corner T.
 S and U cannot be placed on the same side.
Which one of the following statements is correct based on the above
information?

options.A: P cannot be placed at a corner
options.B: S cannot be placed at a corner
options.C: U cannot be placed at a mid-point
options.D: R cannot be placed at a corner

questions.subtopic: Transformation of shapes: translation, rotation, scaling, mirroring, assembling, and grouping
questions.explaination: In a triangle, a segment connecting two midpoints is parallel to the opposite side joining two vertices. Between segments $PR$ and $QS$, one must connect two corners and the other two midpoints. If $S$ were a corner, then $Q$ and $S$ would both be corners, leaving $P$ and $R$ as midpoints, which violates the condition that $S$ and $U$ cannot share a side while $P$ opposes corner $T$. Thus, $S$ cannot be placed at a corner.

individual plots to be similar in shape, not necessarily equal in area. The land
has equally spaced poles, marked as dots in the below figure. Two ropes, R1 and
R2, are already present and cannot be moved.
What is the least number of additional straight ropes needed to create the
desired plots? A single rope can pass through three poles that are aligned in a
straight line.

options.D:

questions.explaination: To partition the rectangular plot into four mutually similar subplots respecting the existing fixed ropes R1 and R2, exactly 3 additional collinear straight rope segments are needed to complete the congruent triangular and trapezoidal subdivisions.

questions.question_text:
Looking at the surface of a smooth 3-dimensional object from the outside, which
one of the following options is TRUE?

options.A: The surface of the object must be concave everywhere.
options.B: The surface of the object must be convex everywhere.
options.C: The surface of the object may be concave in some places and convex in other places.
options.D: The object can have edges, but no corners.

questions.subtopic: Transformation of shapes: translation, rotation, scaling, mirroring, assembling, and grouping
questions.explaination: A smooth 3-dimensional object (such as a torus or a dumbbell shape) can possess regions of positive Gaussian curvature where it is locally convex, as well as regions of negative curvature (saddle-like regions) where it is locally concave. Hence, its surface may be concave in some places and convex in others.

options_latex.A: The surface of the object must be concave everywhere.
options_latex.B: The surface of the object must be convex everywhere.
options_latex.C: The surface of the object may be concave in some places and convex in other places.
options_latex.D: The object can have edges, but no corners.

questions.question_text:
A rectangular paper of 20 cm × 8 cm is folded 3 times. Each fold is made along the
line of symmetry, which is perpendicular to its long edge. The perimeter of the final
folded sheet (in cm) is
questions.subtopic: Paper folding, cutting, and patterns in 2 and 3 dimensions
questions.explaination: Starting at $20 \times 8\text{ cm}$, the 1st fold perpendicular to the long edge yields $10 \times 8\text{ cm}$. The 2nd fold perpendicular to the new long edge ($10\text{ cm}$) yields $5 \times 8\text{ cm}$. The 3rd fold perpendicular to the new long edge ($8\text{ cm}$) yields $5 \times 4\text{ cm}$. The perimeter of this final folded sheet is $2(5 + 4) = 18\text{ cm}$.

questions.question_text:
A cube is to be cut into 8 pieces of equal size and shape. Here, each cut should be
straight and it should not stop till it reaches the other end of the cube.
The minimum number of such cuts required is
questions.subtopic: Paper folding, cutting, and patterns in 2 and 3 dimensions
questions.explaination: A single full planar straight cut can at most double the number of pieces. With $k$ cuts through 3 orthogonal dimensions (1 cut parallel to $xy$-plane, 1 parallel to $yz$-plane, 1 parallel to $zx$-plane), the cube is divided into $2 \times 2 \times 2 = 8$ equal pieces. Thus, a minimum of 3 cuts is required.
